name: Chapter 4: Principles of Inheritance and Variation
description: Mendel’s laws, incomplete and co-dominance, linkage, polygenic traits, pleiotropy, sex determination, mutation and genetic disorders

cards.definition: Branch of biology dealing with inheritance and variation of characters from parents to offspring
Process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny; the basis of heredity
The degree by which progeny differ from their parents

cards.term: Since when did humans know variation was hidden in sexual reproduction?
cards.definition: As early as 8000–1000 B.C.

cards.term: Example of an Indian breed made by artificial selection?
cards.definition: Sahiwal cows in Punjab
Garden pea; seven years (1856–1863)

cards.term: Why was Mendel’s work a first in biology?
cards.definition: First to apply statistical analysis and mathematical logic to biological problems
Large sampling size and confirmation over successive generations
A line that, after continuous self-pollination, shows stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations

cards.term: How many true-breeding pea varieties did Mendel select?
cards.definition: 14 (as 7 pairs differing in one character)

Stem height: Tall / dwarf; Flower colour: Violet / white; Flower position: Axial / terminal; Pod shape: Inflated / constricted; Pod colour: Green / yellow; Seed shape: Round / wrinkled; Seed colour: Yellow / green

cards.term: Identify: seven pairs of traits Mendel studied.
cards.definition: Figure 4.1: seed shape, seed colour, flower colour, pod shape, pod colour, flower position, stem height
"Short Silly Flowers Fly Past Poor Seeds": Stem height, Seed shape, Flower colour, Flower position, Pod shape, Pod colour, Seed colour

cards.term: Pod colour trap: which is dominant?
cards.definition: Green pod is dominant over yellow (opposite of seed colour, where yellow is dominant)

cards.term: Advantages of pea for Mendel’s experiments? (Exercise 1)
cards.definition: Many contrasting traits, naturally self-pollinating, easy to cross-pollinate artificially, short life cycle, many seeds

cards.term: Steps in making a cross in pea (Figure 4.2)?
cards.definition: Remove anthers (emasculation) from the female parent → transfer pollen from the male parent (pollination) → seeds → progeny
All tall; none dwarf
3/4 tall, 1/4 dwarf; no blending (no in-between heights)

cards.term: What did Mendel call the units passed on through gametes?
cards.definition: Factors; now called genes
The units of inheritance; contain information to express a trait
Genes coding for a pair of contrasting traits: slightly different forms of the same gene
Capital letter for the trait expressed in F₁ (T), small letter for the other (t). Never T and d.
Homozygous: identical alleles (TT, tt). Heterozygous: dissimilar alleles (Tt).
Genotype: genetic make-up (TT, Tt, tt). Phenotype: observable trait (tall, dwarf).
In a dissimilar pair, the dominant is expressed; the recessive is masked (expressed only when homozygous)
A cross studying one character (e.g. TT × tt); Tt is a monohybrid

cards.term: How do alleles behave in gamete formation?
cards.definition: They segregate randomly; each gamete gets one allele (50% chance each)

cards.term: Who developed the Punnett square, and what is it?
cards.definition: Reginald C. Punnett; a graphical way to calculate probability of all possible genotypes in a cross

cards.text: Monohybrid F₂: phenotypic ratio {{c1::3 : 1}}; genotypic ratio {{c2::1 : 2 : 1}} (TT : Tt : tt).

cards.term: Binomial form of the monohybrid F₂?
cards.definition: \[(\tfrac12 T + \tfrac12 t)^2 = \tfrac14 TT + \tfrac12 Tt + \tfrac14 tt\]

cards.term: Why can’t you tell TT from Tt by looking? (intuition)
cards.definition: One working allele (T) is enough to make the plant tall: dominance hides the recessive

cards.term: Result of selfing dwarf F₂ plants?
cards.definition: Dwarfs in F₃ and F₄: dwarfs are homozygous tt

cards.term: Self-pollinating a tall F₂ plant would give?
cards.definition: 1/3 of tall F₂ (TT) breed true; 2/3 (Tt) give 3 tall : 1 dwarf
Crossing a dominant phenotype (unknown genotype) with the recessive parent
All dominant → unknown is homozygous. 1 : 1 → unknown is heterozygous.

cards.term: Read Figure 4.5: violet flower × ww gives half violet, half white. Genotype?
cards.definition: Ww (heterozygous)

cards.term: What does the law of dominance explain?
cards.definition: Only one parental character in F₁, both in F₂, and the 3:1 F₂ ratio
Alleles of a pair segregate during gamete formation so each gamete receives only one factor

cards.term: Why is it called the law of "purity of gametes"?
cards.definition: Alleles never blend; each gamete is pure for one allele

cards.term: Gametes from homozygous vs heterozygous parent?
cards.definition: Homozygous: all similar. Heterozygous: two kinds in equal proportion.
F₁ phenotype is in between the two parents
Flower colour in dog flower (snapdragon, Antirrhinum)

cards.term: Snapdragon RR × rr: F₁ and F₂?
cards.definition: F₁ all pink (Rr). F₂ 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

cards.term: Why is incomplete dominance special in ratios?
cards.definition: Phenotypic ratio = genotypic ratio = 1:2:1

cards.term: Molecular view: three possible products of a modified allele?
cards.definition: (i) normal or less efficient enzyme (ii) non-functional enzyme (iii) no enzyme

cards.term: Why is the modified allele usually recessive?
cards.definition: It makes a non-functional or no enzyme; phenotype then depends on the unmodified (functioning) allele, which is dominant
When it still makes a normal/less efficient enzyme: same phenotype (very common)
F₁ resembles both parents: both alleles are expressed
ABO blood groups: alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ both express in AB

cards.term: What does the gene I control?
cards.definition: The kind of sugar polymer protruding from the RBC plasma membrane

cards.term: Alleles of gene I and their products?
cards.definition: Iᴬ and Iᴮ: slightly different sugars. i: no sugar.
Iᴬ and Iᴮ are completely dominant over i; Iᴬ and Iᴮ are co-dominant
IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi: A; IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi: B; IᴬIᴮ: AB; ii: O

cards.term: How many ABO genotypes and phenotypes?
cards.definition: 6 genotypes, 4 phenotypes
More than two alleles governing the same character (e.g. Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i)

cards.term: Why can multiple alleles be found only in population studies?
cards.definition: An individual (diploid) carries only two alleles

cards.term: Child O; father A; mother B. Genotypes? (Exercise 12)
cards.definition: Father Iᴬi, mother Iᴮi. Other children: IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O).

cards.term: Starch synthesis in pea: BB, Bb, bb seeds?
cards.definition: BB: large starch grains, round. bb: small grains, wrinkled. Bb: round seeds but intermediate grains.

cards.term: What does the pea starch gene show about dominance?
cards.definition: Seed shape: B is dominant. Starch grain size: incomplete dominance. Dominance depends on the phenotype chosen.

cards.term: Is dominance an autonomous feature of a gene?
cards.definition: No. It depends on the gene product and on the particular phenotype examined

cards.term: Dihybrid cross: parents and F₁ in Mendel’s example?
cards.definition: RRYY (round yellow) × rryy (wrinkled green) → F₁ RrYy (round yellow)

cards.term: Dominant traits in the dihybrid cross?
cards.definition: Yellow over green, round over wrinkled

cards.text: Dihybrid F₂ phenotypic ratio: {{c1::9}} round yellow : {{c2::3}} wrinkled yellow : {{c2::3}} round green : {{c3::1}} wrinkled green.

cards.definition: \[(3:1) \times (3:1)\](3 round : 1 wrinkled)(3 yellow : 1 green)

cards.term: State the law of independent assortment.
cards.definition: When two pairs of traits combine in a hybrid, segregation of one pair is independent of the other pair

cards.term: Gametes from RrYy and their frequency?
cards.definition: RY, Ry, rY, ry, each 1/4

cards.term: Dihybrid F₂: number of genotypes and phenotypes?
cards.definition: 9 genotypes, 4 phenotypes (in 16 squares)

cards.term: Types of gametes from an organism heterozygous at 4 loci? (Exercise 3)
cards.definition: \( 2^n = 2^4 = \) 16
Tall green 3/8; dwarf green 1/8

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 7

TtYy × Ttyy: fraction tall and green?

Treat each gene separately, then multiply.
  1. Tt × Tt → 3/4 tall, 1/4 dwarf
  2. Yy × yy → 1/2 yellow, 1/2 green
  3. ?
  4. Dwarf and green = 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 7

TtYy × Ttyy: fraction tall and green?

Treat each gene separately, then multiply.
  1. Tt × Tt → 3/4 tall, 1/4 dwarf
  2. Yy × yy → 1/2 yellow, 1/2 green
  3. Tall and green = 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8
  4. Dwarf and green = 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8

cards.definition: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1

cards.term: When did Mendel publish, and when was it recognised?
cards.definition: Published 1865; unrecognised till 1900
Poor communication discrete non-blending factors vs apparent continuous variation maths in biology unacceptable no physical proof of factors
de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak (independently)

cards.term: By when was chromosome movement in meiosis worked out?
cards.definition: 1902

cards.term: Who noted chromosome behaviour parallels gene behaviour?
cards.definition: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri

cards.term: Who proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance? (Exercise 15)
cards.definition: Sutton (with Boveri): united chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles

cards.term: Parallel behaviour of genes and chromosomes
cards.definition: Pairs: Occur in pairs; Gamete formation: Segregate; one of each pair to a gamete; Two pairs: Segregate independently of each other

cards.term: Where are the two alleles of a gene located?
cards.definition: At homologous sites on homologous chromosomes

cards.term: How do chromosomes explain independent assortment?
cards.definition: In meiosis I, two chromosome pairs align at the metaphase plate independently (Possibility I or II)

cards.term: Who experimentally verified the chromosomal theory?
cards.definition: Thomas Hunt Morgan and colleagues

cards.term: Why was Drosophila ideal for genetics?
cards.definition: Grown on simple synthetic medium life cycle ~2 weeks many progeny per mating sexes easy to tell apart many visible hereditary variations
Yellow-bodied white-eyed females × brown-bodied red-eyed males; F₂ deviated from 9:3:3:1
On the X chromosome
Physical association of genes on a chromosome (term coined by Morgan)
Generation of non-parental gene combinations

cards.term: When two genes are on the same chromosome, which combinations dominate?
cards.definition: Parental combinations are much higher than non-parental

cards.text: White and yellow genes: {{c1::1.3}}% recombination (tightly linked); white and miniature wing: {{c2::37.2}}% (loosely linked).

cards.definition: Tight: genes close, very low recombination. Loose: genes far apart, higher recombination.

cards.term: Who made the first genetic map, and how?
cards.definition: Alfred Sturtevant (Morgan’s student): used recombination frequency as a measure of gene distance

cards.term: Why does recombination frequency measure distance? (intuition)
cards.definition: Crossing over can happen anywhere; the farther apart two genes are, the more likely a crossover falls between them
Starting point for whole-genome sequencing (e.g. Human Genome Project)
Verified chromosomal theory; discovered linkage, recombination and sex-linked inheritance in Drosophila

cards.term: Two heterozygous parents, loci completely linked: F₁ ratio? (Exercise 8)
cards.definition: Like a monohybrid: 3 : 1 (only parental combinations; with some recombination, parental types exceed recombinants)
Traits controlled by three or more genes, spread across a gradient; also influenced by environment
Human height, human skin colour

cards.term: How do alleles act in a polygenic trait?
cards.definition: Each allele’s effect is additive

cards.term: Skin colour model with A, B, C: darkest and lightest?
cards.definition: AABBCC darkest aabbcc lightest three dominant + three recessive = intermediate
A single gene with multiple phenotypic expressions
The gene affects a metabolic pathway contributing to different phenotypes
Phenylketonuria: mutation in phenylalanine hydroxylase gene → mental retardation + reduced hair and skin pigmentation
Poly-genic = many genes → one trait. Pleio-tropy = one gene → many traits.

cards.term: Who first saw the "X body", and in what?
cards.definition: Henking (1891), during spermatogenesis in insects; 50% sperms received it
The X chromosome
Sex chromosomes: differ between sexes and determine sex. Autosomes: all the rest.
Grasshopper: male XO (one X), female XX. Males have one fewer chromosome.
Humans, Drosophila, many insects and mammals; male XY, female XX
Males produce two kinds of gametes (X/O or X/Y): XO and XY types

cards.term: ZW type: example and heterogametic sex?
cards.definition: Birds: female ZW (heterogametic), male ZZ

cards.term: In birds, who decides the chick’s sex?
cards.definition: The egg (female makes Z or W eggs)
XO (grasshopper): XO / XX; XY (humans, Drosophila): XY / XX; ZW (birds): ZZ / ZW; Haplodiploid (honey bee): n (16) / 2n (32)

cards.definition: 23 pairs: 22 pairs autosomes + XX (female) or XY (male)

cards.term: Why does the father determine the baby’s sex?
cards.definition: 50% sperms carry X, 50% carry Y; all ova carry X

cards.term: Probability of a boy in each pregnancy?
cards.definition: 50%

cards.term: Basis of sex determination in honey bee?
cards.definition: Number of sets of chromosomes (haplodiploidy)

cards.term: Honey bee: fertilised vs unfertilised egg?
cards.definition: Fertilised → female (queen or worker), 32 chromosomes. Unfertilised → male (drone) by parthenogenesis, 16.
By mitosis (they are already haploid)
No father, cannot have sons; but has a grandfather and can have grandsons
Alteration of DNA sequence changing genotype and phenotype

cards.term: Two sources of variation in DNA?
cards.definition: Recombination and mutation

cards.term: How do deletions/insertions cause chromosomal aberrations?
cards.definition: One DNA helix runs through each chromatid; losing or gaining a segment alters the chromosome

cards.term: Where are chromosomal aberrations commonly seen?
cards.definition: In cancer cells

cards.term: What is a point mutation? Example? (Exercise 14)
cards.definition: Change in a single base pair; e.g. sickle-cell anaemia
Deletion or insertion of base pairs
Chemical and physical factors inducing mutation; e.g. UV radiation
Analysis of a trait over several generations of a family, drawn as a family tree

cards.term: Why is pedigree analysis needed in humans? (Exercise 10)
cards.definition: Controlled crosses are not possible in humans; it traces inheritance of a trait, abnormality or disease

masks.answer: Parents above, children below (birth order left to right)

cards.term: Correction: NCERT labels both the honey bee figure and the pedigree symbols as "Figure 4.13". Note?
cards.definition: A numbering slip: the pedigree symbols figure should be 4.14 (and the next ones shift by one)
Mendelian (single gene) and chromosomal
Haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia

cards.term: Identify the traits in these pedigrees (Figure 4.14).
cards.definition: (a) Autosomal dominant (e.g. myotonic dystrophy) (b) autosomal recessive (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia)
Affected child from two unaffected parents (both carriers); often skips generations
Mostly males affected, passed via carrier mothers; never father to son

Colour blindness: X-linked recessive; Haemophilia: X-linked recessive; Sickle-cell anaemia: Autosomal recessive; Phenylketonuria: Autosomal recessive; Thalassemia: Autosomal recessive; Myotonic dystrophy: Autosomal dominant

cards.definition: Defect in red or green cone due to mutation in genes on the X chromosome; cannot distinguish red and green
About 8% of males, 0.4% of females

cards.term: Why is colour blindness commoner in males?
cards.definition: Males have only one X; one recessive allele is enough

cards.term: Son of a carrier mother: chance of colour blindness?
cards.definition: 50%

cards.term: When can a daughter be colour blind?
cards.definition: Mother is at least a carrier and father is colour blind
A single protein of the blood-clotting cascade is affected: a simple cut causes non-stop bleeding

cards.term: Why are haemophilic females extremely rare?
cards.definition: Mother must be at least a carrier and father haemophilic (who rarely survives to later life)
Queen Victoria
HbᴬHbᴬ normal HbᴬHbˢ carrier (sickle-cell trait) HbˢHbˢ diseased
Glutamic acid → valine at the 6th position of the β-globin chain
Sixth codon GAG → GUG (single base substitution)

cards.term: Correction: NCERT gives "GAG to GUG" for the gene. Precise statement?
cards.definition: GUG is the mRNA codon; in the DNA coding strand it is GAG → GTG (A→T)
Mutant Hb polymerises under low O₂ tension; RBC changes from biconcave disc to sickle shape

cards.term: Why is sickle-cell trait common in malaria areas? (beyond NCERT)
cards.definition: Carriers (HbᴬHbˢ) resist malaria: heterozygote advantage keeps the allele in the population
Lacks the enzyme converting phenylalanine → tyrosine phenylalanine → phenylpyruvic acid accumulates in brain → mental retardation excreted in urine
Mutation or deletion → reduced synthesis of α or β globin chains → abnormal Hb → anaemia

cards.term: α vs β thalassemia: genes and chromosome?
cards.definition: α: HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 (4 genes). β: HBB on chromosome 11.
The more genes affected (of four), the less α-globin made
Thalassemia: quantitative (too few globin). Sickle-cell: qualitative (incorrectly functioning globin).
Sickle-cell anaemia: sickled RBCs, anaemia. Phenylketonuria: mental retardation, light pigmentation.
Absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes

cards.term: What is aneuploidy, and its cause?
cards.definition: Gain or loss of chromosome(s), due to failure of segregation of chromatids

cards.term: What is polyploidy, and its cause?
cards.definition: Increase in a whole set of chromosomes, due to failure of cytokinesis after telophase; common in plants
Trisomy: an extra copy of a chromosome (2n+1). Monosomy: one chromosome of a pair missing (2n−1).
Trisomy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes)
Langdon Down (1866)
Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with palm crease, retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development
47, XXY
Masculine development with feminine traits (gynaecomastia), tall; sterile
45, XO
Sterile female, rudimentary ovaries, short stature, lack of secondary sexual characters
(a) Klinefelter (tall, feminised). (b) Turner (short, underdeveloped feminine character).
Klinefelter = eXtra X in a male (XXY). Turner = a female who "turned" in one X (XO).
Down’s syndrome: 47, +21 (trisomy 21); Klinefelter’s: 47, XXY; Turner’s: 45, XO
